title: Lease & Failover Safeguards for Reserved Pools (Dedicated Capacity PRD)
creator: Aisha Kumar
description: Problem statement: Customers running production workloads on Redwood Dedicated report unpredictable degradation during transient hotspots and preemption events. Reserved pools today are inflexible: long commit windows, blunt eviction, and opaque fallback behavior lead to failed requests, unexpected latency spikes, and escalations. This PRD defines lease semantics, graceful fallback paths, and autoscale/ burst-handling rules to make reserved capacity predictable and actionable for enterprise customers.
goals: Introduce a short-term lease mechanism (seconds->minutes) to allow safe transient borrowing and automatic reconciliation with long-term reservations
Define deterministic fallback rules when reserved pool capacity is exhausted: warm handoff to compatible model variants or shared fairshare with tiered QoS
Provide per-tenant isolation profiles and a simple UI/ API to tune burst tolerance and preemption sensitivity
Ship telemetry and alerting that tie SLA violations to tenant lease events and fallback triggers
success_metrics: Reduce customer-visible failed requests during transient surge by >= 80% for tenants using leases
Lower 95th percentile latency tail on heavy-burst tenants by 30% under peak load
Decrease inbound production escalations related to evaporation or opaque evictions by 50% in first quarter post-release
Coverage: 90% of Dedicated customers have default lease-enabled fallback config applied to new reservations
user_personas: Platform engineer at customer: needs predictable latency and graceful fallbacks during traffic spikes
SaaS product engineer: cares about API error surface and predictable throttling semantics
Redwood oncall/infra owner: needs clear signals to diagnose evictions and capacity handoffs
requirements: API: reservation creation accepts optional leasePolicy {leaseWindowSec, maxBorrowPct, preemptible:true|false, fallbackPriority}
Runtime: implement lease allocator that grants short-term capacity up to maxBorrowPct of reserved pool for leaseWindowSec with TTL and auto-reconcile

Fallback: route requests exceeding reserved+lease capacity to (in order) 1) compatible lower-cost model variant in same region, 2) shared fairshare pool with tenant-tier weight, 3) reject with structured error containing recovery ETA
Autoscaling: reservation autoscaler evaluates warm-up signals and preemptively request hot pools when sustained borrow > 50% for >60s, with safety caps

Observability: expose token-level cost and latency attribution for lease vs reserved vs fallback handling in Console; emit events to audit log with tenant, reservation_id, action (lease_grant, lease_reconcile, fallback_used, preempted), and reason codes
Operator controls: console toggle to opt-out of lease borrowing per-customer, and an emergency preempt policy to force-evict borrowed leases with configurable grace period
Backward compatibility: default behavior remains current (no leases) unless admin or reservation API enables leasePolicy
non_goals: Not introducing new multi-region live-migration of KV caches in this phase
Not changing core billing model for reserved capacity in release v1 (billing flows will be clarified in follow-up)
Not reworking long-term commit contracts (monthly/annual) — this focuses on short-term lease behavior
scope_changes: 2025-02-08: Added operator emergency preempt policy after design review — requirement requested by SRE
2025-02-12: Narrowed autoscaler trigger to 60s sustained borrow (from initial 30s) after performance modelling showed oscillation risk
2025-02-14: Post-legal review, added structured fallback error with ETA and documentation updates for contract teams
rollout_plan: Phase 0 (canary): internal Redwood tenants + 3 pilot customers — enable leases for non-critical reservations, collect telemetry (2 weeks)
Phase 1 (controlled): opt-in by customer admins via Console and API; enable fallback routing in read-only mode to measure impact (4 weeks)
Phase 2 (default opt-in): new reservations default to lease-enabled with visible console policy; existing customers remain opt-out unless they flip toggle (6 weeks)
Rollback plan: if error rate or latency regresses beyond thresholds, disable lease allocator and revert routing to current behavior; emit incident timeline and rollback checklist
acceptance_criteria: End-to-end: Given a reservation with leasePolicy (leaseWindowSec=300, maxBorrowPct=20), under 120s spike we observe lease_grant events and no request rejections for up to configured borrow pct
Fallback: When reserved+lease capacity exceeded, runtime routes requests to a preconfigured compatible variant and the client receives structured error only when all fallbacks exhausted
Telemetry: Console shows per-reservation metrics for lease usage, fallback counts, and median/95p latency for each path
Ops: SREs can trigger emergency preempt and observe borrowed capacity reclaimed within configured grace period and audit logs populated
Security: Audit log entries for lease grants and fallbacks comply with retention and tamper-resistance controls required by compliance team
Tests: Unit and integration tests cover lease TTL expiry, reconcile loop correctness, and autoscaler hysteresis to prevent oscillation
dependencies: ENG-34899: fallback routing and model compatibility mapping
ENG-35500: console telemetry surface and audit log plumbing
PM-100300: billing clarification for short-term borrow (follow-up)
notes: Design tradeoff: We prefer short leases over immediate preemption to reduce user-visible errors; risk is a small increase in transient overcommit that autoscaler must absorb
Implementation note: lease grants should be idempotent and keyed by request digest to avoid double-counting under retry
PM decision log: default opt-in chosen to encourage adoption while providing enterprise opt-out
Follow-ups: Billing changes, longer-term multi-region cache migration, and an API for programmatic lease tuning
